source_text: Habes igitur Dei mei voluntatem: occursum est huic plagae. In alium ictum consideremus, de voluntatis qualitate. Longum est ut Deum meum bonum ostendam, quod jam a nobis didicerunt Marcionitae. Deum interim sufficit dici, ut necesse sit bonum credi. Malum enim Deum qui praesumpserit, constare in utroque non poterit: aut Deum negare debebit, quem malum existimarit; aut bonum dicere, quem Deum pronuntiarit. Bona igitur erit et voluntas ejus, qui nisi bonus, non erit Deus. Probabit hoc etiam ipsius rei bonitas, quam Deus voluit; martyrii dico: quia bonum nonnisi bonus voluit. Bonum contendo martyrium apud eumdem Deum, a quo et prohibetur et punitur idololatria. Obnititur enim et adversatur idololatriae martyrium. Malo autem obniti et adversari nisi bonum non potest. Non quasi negemus esse aemulationem, tam malorum inter se, quam et bonorum. Sed alia conditio est hujus tituli. Martyrium enim non de communi aliqua malitia certat cum idololatria, sed de sua gratia; liberat enim ab idololatria. Quod a malo liberat, quis non bonum pronuntiabit? quid aliud est adversatio idololatriae atque martyrii, quam mortis et vitae? In tantum vita martyrio deputabitur, quantum mors idololatriae. Vitam qui malum dixerit, habet mortem quam bonum dicat. Est et haec perversitas hominum, salutaria excutere, exitiosa suscipere, periculosa quaerere, medica male vitare; mori denique citius, quam curari desiderare. Nam et medicinae praesidium plures refugiunt: plures enim stulti, plures timidi, et male verecundi. Et est plane quasi saevitia medicinae, de scalpello, deque cauterio, de sinapis incendio; non tamen secari, et inuri, et extendi, idcirco malum, quia dolores utiles affert: nec quia tantummodo contristat, recusabitur; sed quia necessario contristat, adhibebitur. Horrorem operis fructus excusat. Ululans denique ille, et gemens, et mugiens inter manus medici, postmodum easdem mercede cumulabit, artifices optimas praedicabit, et saevas jam negabit. Sic et martyria desaeviunt, sed in salutem; licebit et Deo in vitam aeternam per ignes et gladios et acerba quaeque curare. Sed medicum quidem miraberis etiam in illo, quod ferme pares adhibet qualitates medelarum adversus qualitates querelarum: cum quasi de perverso auxiliatur, per ea subveniens per quae laboratur. Nam et calores caloribus amplius onerando compescit, et ardores siti potius macerando restinguit, et fellis excessus amaris quibusque potiunculis colligit, et sanguinis fluxus defusa insuper venula revocat. Deum vero, et quidem zelotem, culpandum existimabis, si voluit certasse cum caussa, et injuriae aemulando prodesse, mortem morte dissolvere, occisionem occisione dispargere, tormentis tormenta discutere, supplicia suppliciis evaporare, vitam auferendo conferre, carnem laedendo juvare, animam eripiendo servare. Perversitas quam putas, ratio est; quod saevitiam existimas, gratia est: ita Deo de momentaneis aeterna medicante. Magnifica bono tuo Deum tetrum: incidisti in manus ejus, sed feliciter incidisti; incidit et ille in aegritudines tuas. Homo semper medico prior negotium facit: denique sibimetipse periculum mortis attraxit. Acceperat a Domino suo, ut a medico, satis utilem disciplinam secundum legem vivendi, ut omnia quidem ederet, ab una solummodo arbuscula temperaret, quam ipse medicus importunam interim noverat: audiit ille quem maluit, et abstinentiam rupit, edit illicitum, et transgressione saturatus, in mortem cruditavit, dignissimus bona fide in totum perire, qui voluit. Sed Dominus sustentata fervura delicti, donec tempore medicina temperaretur, paulatim remedia composuit, omnes fidei disciplinas, et ipsas aemulas vitio, verbum mortis verbo vitae rescindentes, auditum transgressionis auditu devotionis limantes, ita et cum mori praecipit medicus ille, veternum mortis excludit. Quid gravatur pati nunc homo ex remedio, quod non est tunc gravatus pati ex vitio? displicet occidi in salutem, cui non displicuit occidi in perditionem? nauseabit ad antidotum, qui hiavit ad venenum?
pass_a_gloss: You have, therefore, the will of my God: a remedy has been found for this affliction. Let us consider another blow, concerning the quality of the will. It is a long task to show that my God is good, which the Marcionites have already learned from us. For the time being, it is enough to say that God is good, so that it is necessary to believe that He is good. For the one who presumes that God is evil cannot consistently hold both views: either he must deny that God exists, whom he considers evil; or he must say that the one he calls God is good. Therefore, the will of the one who is good, unless He is good, will not be God. The goodness of the thing that God wills also proves this, I mean martyrdom: because only a good God wills what is good. I argue that martyrdom is good in the eyes of the same God, by whom idolatry is also prohibited and punished. For martyrdom resists and opposes idolatry. But only what is good can resist and oppose evil. We do not deny that there is a rivalry between evils and between goods. But the condition of this title is different. For martyrdom does not compete with idolatry over some common evil, but over its own grace; it frees from idolatry. What frees from evil, who would not call good? What is the opposition of idolatry and martyrdom, if not death and life? To the extent that life is attributed to martyrdom, to that extent death is attributed to idolatry. The one who says that life is evil has death, which he calls good. There is also this perversity of men, to reject what is salutary, to accept what is destructive, to seek what is dangerous, to avoid what is medicinal; finally, to desire to die rather than to be cured. For many people also shun the aid of medicine: many are foolish, many are timid, and many are improperly shamefaced. And it is almost as if the cruelty of medicine, with its scalpel, cauterization, and burning with sinapism; nevertheless, to be cut, burned, and stretched is not evil, because it brings useful pains: nor is it rejected because it causes sadness, but because it necessarily causes sadness, it is applied. The horror of the work is excused by its fruit. Finally, the one who cries out, groans, and bellows in the hands of the doctor, afterwards will heap praise on the same doctors, will call them excellent artisans, and will no longer call them cruel. So also martyrdom seems cruel, but it is for salvation; it is permitted for God to cure through fires, swords, and bitter things, for eternal life. But you will also marvel at the doctor, who for the most part applies equal qualities of remedies against the qualities of the complaints: when, as it were, he helps through perverse means, by assisting through the very things by which one suffers. For he restrains fevers by applying greater heat, and extinguishes burning by inducing thirst, and collects excess bile with bitter drinks, and recalls the flow of blood by applying a vein on top. But you will think that God, and indeed a zealous God, is to be blamed, if He wills to contend with the cause, and by rivaling the injury, to be of benefit, to dissolve death by death, to dispel killing by killing, to shake off torments by torments, to evaporate punishments by punishments, to confer life by taking it away, to help by wounding the flesh, to save by taking away the soul. The perversity that you think, is reason; what you consider cruelty, is grace: thus God, who is eternal, medicates through temporary means. Praise your good God, even if He seems harsh: you have fallen into His hands, but you have fallen in happily; He has also fallen into your afflictions. Man always makes a deal with the doctor beforehand: finally, he has drawn danger to himself. He had received from his Lord, as from a doctor, a very useful discipline according to the law of living, so that he might eat all things, but abstain from only one tree, which the doctor Himself knew was troublesome: he listened to the one he preferred, and broke his abstention, ate what was forbidden, and having been satiated by transgression, he became crude in death, most worthy of perishing entirely, because he willed it. But the Lord, having sustained the fervor of the sin, until the time when the medicine was tempered, gradually composed remedies, all the disciplines of faith, and those that rival vice, rescinding the word of death with the word of life, cleansing the hearing of transgression with the hearing of devotion, so that even when the doctor commands one to die, he excludes eternal death. Why does man now hesitate to suffer from the remedy, when he was not hesitant to suffer from vice? Does it displease him to be killed for salvation, when it did not displease him to be killed in perdition? Will he be nauseated by the antidote, who has devoured poison?

pass_b_english: So you have my God's will: a remedy has been found for this affliction. Now let us consider another blow, concerning the quality of that will. It would take too long to prove my God is good; the Marcionites have already learned that from us. For now, it is enough to say 'God,' which forces the conclusion that He is good. Anyone who presumes God is evil cannot hold both positions: either he must deny the existence of the God he calls evil, or he must admit that the one he calls God is good. Therefore, the will of the One who is good is good—unless He is good, He is not God. The goodness of what God wills also proves this; I mean martyrdom, because only a good God wills what is good. I argue that martyrdom is good before the same God who prohibits and punishes idolatry. Martyrdom resists and opposes idolatry, but nothing evil can resist evil—only what is good can. We do not deny there is rivalry among evils and among goods, but this case is different. Martyrdom does not compete with idolatry over some common wickedness; it competes over its own grace, because it frees from idolatry. Who would not call good that which frees from evil? What is the opposition between idolatry and martyrdom if not death and life? Life is credited to martyrdom to the same degree that death is credited to idolatry. The man who calls life evil has death, which he calls good. This is the perversity of men: to reject what saves, accept what destroys, seek danger, avoid the cure, and finally desire death rather than healing. Many also shun medical help—fools, cowards, and the falsely modest. Medicine seems cruel with its scalpel, cautery, and burning mustard plasters, yet being cut, seared, and stretched is not evil because it brings useful pain. It is not rejected because it causes sorrow; because it necessarily causes sorrow, it is applied. The horror of the procedure is excused by its fruit. The patient who screams, groans, and bellows under the doctor's hands will afterward heap those same hands with praise, call them master artisans, and deny they were ever cruel. So martyrdoms also rage, but for salvation; God may cure through fires, swords, and every bitter thing for eternal life. You will marvel at the Doctor too: He mostly applies remedies whose qualities match the complaints—helping through perverse means, by the very things through which we suffer. He checks fevers by piling on greater heat, quenches burning by inducing thirst, gathers excess bile with bitter draughts, and recalls the flow of blood by opening a vein. Yet you would blame God, even a zealous God, if He chooses to contend with the cause and benefit by rivaling the injury: dissolving death by death, scattering killing by killing, shaking off torments by torments, evaporating punishments by punishments, conferring life by taking it, helping by wounding the flesh, saving by taking the soul. What you call perversity is reason; what you call cruelty is grace: thus the eternal God heals through temporary means. Praise your good God, however harsh He seems: you have fallen into His hands, but happily; He has also fallen into your afflictions. Man always strikes the bargain with the doctor first; in the end, he draws the danger of death upon himself. He had received from his Lord, as from a physician, a most useful discipline for living under the law (Genesis 2:16-17): he might eat of every tree, but abstain from only one, which the Doctor Himself knew was trouble. He listened to the voice he preferred, broke his fast, ate the forbidden fruit, and gorged on transgression until he grew raw in death—most worthy to perish utterly, because he chose it. But the Lord, sustaining the heat of the sin until the medicine was ready, gradually compounded remedies: all the disciplines of faith, even those rivaling vice—rescinding the word of death with the word of life, scraping the hearing of transgression clean with the hearing of devotion—so that even when the Doctor commands death, He excludes eternal death. Why does man now balk at suffering from the remedy, when he never balked at suffering from vice? Does it displease him to be killed for salvation, when it did not displease him to be killed for perdition? Will he gag on the antidote who swallowed poison?

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex medical metaphors and the theological argument regarding God's goodness and the nature of martyrdom. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Latin source. The addition of (Genesis 2:16-17) in Pass B is a correct identification of the allusion to the forbidden tree.
